clinical.title: Clinical phenotype & endpoints — Prexasertib in platinum-resistant BRCA-wild-type HGSOC
clinical.Question: What do the public trial record and primary report actually show, and which patient and biopsy denominators can support a clinical or translational claim?
clinical.Answer: This was an early-terminated signal-seeking study, not a clean efficacy failure or a validated resistance-biomarker study. Forty-nine participants were treated, 39 were RECIST-evaluable, and 12 had a partial response: ORR was 30.8% (12/39; 95% CI 17.0–47.6) among evaluable participants and 24.5% (12/49; exact 95% CI 13.3–38.9) by intention to treat. The planned evaluable denominators were not reached. Only 24 participants had baseline biopsies, 17 had RNA sequencing, and 15 entered the post-hoc transcriptomic analysis, so the clinical response and biomarker claims arise from different populations [PMID 38555285; NCT02203513].
clinical.Interpretation: The clinical record supports a bounded activity signal in heavily pretreated platinum-resistant HGSOC. It does not support calling prexasertib inactive: 12 objective responses were observed. It also does not support calling the regimen effective under the planned phase-2 decision rule, because both cohorts stopped short of their target sample sizes. The translational result is exploratory. The audited source-column linkage permits a bounded same-cohort PFS reanalysis, but a 15-biopsy, post-hoc split cannot validate a selection biomarker. This is a post-publication reanalysis of the same 15 patients used to generate the published hypothesis. It may test a within-cohort association with published PFS, but it is not independent replication or prospective biomarker validation and does not establish resistance mechanism, predictive utility, or treatment interaction. The larger multicenter study makes that limit more important: its lower platinum-resistant ORR and negative genomic screen argue against treating the small trial's 30.8% evaluable ORR or any single baseline alteration as transportable. The CA125 paper does not fill the mechanism gap because it measures response after treatment has started. Its useful question is narrower—whether lack of a confirmed CA125 decline can prospectively flag low probability of RECIST response without making a treatment decision.

pharmacology.title: Mechanism & biomarker biology — What the DNA-replication signal does and does not show
pharmacology.Question: Why did some patients benefit from prexasertib while others did not, and does the public evidence support a clinically usable DNA-replication biomarker or a causal POLA1 resistance mechanism?
pharmacology.Answer: The public data do not explain the patient split. The paper's KEGG DNA-replication enrichment is real as a computation: its gene ranks and weighted enrichment score can be reconstructed from the same 15 biopsies to floating-point precision. But it was discovered with a post-hoc PFS endpoint in those same 15 patients. When the fixed KEGG set is tested across all 5,005 possible 9-versus-6 patient allocations, the result is not unusual (p=0.105). A separate, HGNC-reconciled Reactome patient score is also small and imprecise (Hedges g=0.28, 95% bootstrap CI -0.62 to 1.37, exact allocation p=0.586). This is a reproducible hypothesis, not a validated resistance biomarker. POLA1 perturbation is the strongest orthogonal support. In two parental HGSOC lineages and their acquired prexasertib-resistant derivatives, siPOLA1 plus prexasertib suppressed relative growth more than a descriptive Bliss-independence reference. That supports a controlled causal experiment. It does not establish four independent models, tumor selectivity, direct ST1926–POLA1 engagement, an exposure-feasible drug combination, or a therapeutic window. The full ST1926 response surfaces are reported in Pharmacology & Exposure; they are not biomarker-validation evidence.
pharmacology.Interpretation: The strongest statement is narrow: the paper's KEGG enrichment statistic is reproducible, and the POLA1 genetic-perturbation result makes the biology worth testing. The public evidence does not show that baseline DNA-replication expression predicts which patients benefit from prexasertib. It cannot separate treatment resistance from prognosis, tumor composition, exposure, dose intensity, or other unmeasured patient factors. It also cannot show that inhibiting POLA1 would be tolerable in normal proliferative tissues. Do not select patients or propose a clinical POLA1 combination from this dataset. Freeze one continuous assay, score orientation, QC procedure, endpoint, and pass criterion prospectively—without deriving a clinical cutoff in this cohort—then test the association in an independent prexasertib cohort. A treatment-selection claim would still require a randomized treatment-by-biomarker interaction. Run a therapeutic-index experiment before advancing the combination hypothesis.

adme.title: Pharmacology & exposure — Prexasertib in platinum-resistant HGSOC
adme.Question: Is prexasertib pharmacologically active at plausible human exposure, could heterogeneous exposure explain apparent non-response, and what does the ST1926 combination evidence actually establish?
adme.Answer: Prexasertib is a potent CHK1 inhibitor with an explicit selectivity boundary: the FDA briefing reports CHK1 enzyme IC50 <1 nM, binding Ki 0.9 nM, and CHK2 and p90S6 kinase inhibition below 10 nM in a 224-kinase panel [Prexasertib]. The public evidence makes regimen-level underexposure less likely, but it cannot test whether an individual nonresponder was underexposed. In an external 12-patient phase-1 study, geometric mean AUC(0–72) at 105 mg/m² was 2,160 ng·h/mL at cycle 1 (n=6; CV 13%) and 2,270 ng·h/mL at cycle 2 (n=3; CV 22%), both above the 1,896 ng·h/mL exposure predicted from a Calu-6 xenograft model. Eight of nine reported 105-mg/m² AUC observations across the two cycles exceeded that target [PMC6247064]. That is not exposure–response evidence for NCT02203513. The ovarian trial used the same starting regimen, 105 mg/m² intravenously every two weeks, but exposes no participant-linked concentrations, individual PK estimates, dose intensity, target engagement, or PK-to-response record. A public exposure–response model would therefore manufacture an answer from the wrong population and was not fit [PMID 38555285; analysis/adme/exposure_modelability.json ]. The complete public ST1926-by-prexasertib tumor-cell surfaces support a preclinical interaction hypothesis, not formal synergy or a therapeutic window. The source has unresolved replicate independence and dose-label conflicts, and it contains no matched normal-cell, in-vivo, or combination-exposure data [PMC10981752_SOURCE_DATA].
adme.Interpretation: The measured potency, full tumor-cell response surfaces, and external PK make the mechanism and regimen experimentally plausible. They do not establish that ST1926 engages POLA1, that the combination is exposure-feasible, or that it has a normal-tissue margin. The external PK data argue against a simple claim that the 105-mg/m² regimen was generally too low to reach the sponsor's nonclinical systemic-exposure target. They do not exclude clinically meaningful interpatient variability, dose-intensity loss, tissue-exposure differences, or exposure-independent resistance in the ovarian cohort. The development consequence is narrow: retain exposure as an unresolved alternative explanation, but do not use it to explain the responder split until the sponsor-linked PK package is available. The next analysis should estimate exposure–efficacy and exposure–toxicity jointly; fitting only the response side would ignore the hematologic constraint that shaped actual dosing.

toxicology.title: Toxicology & therapeutic window — Prexasertib
toxicology.Question: What limited prexasertib dosing, and does the public evidence establish a therapeutic window for adding a second replication-stress agent?
toxicology.Answer: Prexasertib dosing was constrained by acute hematologic toxicity. Among 49 treated participants, grade 3 or 4 treatment-related neutropenia occurred in 42 (85.7%), leukocytopenia in 38 (77.6%), thrombocytopenia in 20 (40.8%), anemia in 15 (30.6%), and febrile neutropenia in 6 (12.2%). Eleven participants (22.4%) had a toxicity-related dose reduction and three (6.1%) discontinued for toxicity; no on-treatment deaths were reported [PMID 38555285 Supplementary Data 2]. The public evidence does not establish a numeric combination window. The pharmacology chapter shows real tumor-cell interaction data for ST1926 plus prexasertib, but there are no matched hematopoietic-progenitor or GI-organoid surfaces, participant-linked exposure–toxicity data, in-vivo combination toxicology, or combination-treated patients. Tumor-cell growth inhibition is therefore not treated as toxicology evidence.
toxicology.Interpretation: The principal known clinical constraint is predictable, often severe, and monitorable marrow toxicity. Its transient nature and use of G-CSF made monotherapy delivery possible, but that does not create unused safety margin for a second replication inhibitor. The public data cannot supply a defensible numeric combination margin. That number must be frozen before CRO execution—on an exposure-normalized tumor-versus-marrow/GI scale—so an unfavorable result cannot be rescued by moving the goalpost after the assays are read. The POLA1 result in the pharmacology chapter merits a preclinical falsification program, not a clinical combination proposal. The decisive toxicology weakness is that the same biological strategy that can deepen tumor replication stress can also injure proliferating marrow and GI tissues. Until a clinically qualified POLA1-directed agent demonstrates adequate exposure, target engagement, and a measured normal-tissue window, the public evidence does not support a clinical combination.
